strengths: TAVP addresses a relevant visual manipulation problem by combining learned virtual viewpoints with task-conditioned expert routing. Optimizing rendered representations using downstream action losses is a potentially useful extension of RVT-2 and ARP.

Table 1 reports 86.7% average success across 18 RLBench tasks, compared with 84.9% for ARP+. Several improvements are substantial: insert peg increases from 78.4% to 96%, and sort shape from 46.4% to 64%. These results support the practical promise of the approach.

The pseudo-environment uses existing demonstrations to train viewpoint selection without additional simulator rollouts. This is a sensible training design, although its efficiency advantage is not quantified.

The paper includes component ablations, viewpoint sensitivity experiments, inference timings, and qualitative demonstrations on five real-world tasks. The reported latency increase from 0.394 to 0.436 seconds is modest.
weaknesses: The central viewpoint contribution is not adequately isolated. Table 2 replaces learned views with random views and labels the intervention as removing active-exploration fine-tuning, leaving the training protocol ambiguous. The resulting 8.89% success does not establish superiority over a properly trained fixed-view version with identical TaskMoE architecture and training budget. A matched fixed-view control is especially important because the full model improves over ARP+ by only 1.78 percentage points.

The evidence does not establish the reliability of the aggregate improvement. TAVP is evaluated on 25 episodes per task, without reported repeated training runs or uncertainty estimates; the baseline evaluation and aggregation protocols are insufficiently explained. Results are also mixed: stack cups drops from 80% to 60%, place cups from 48.8% to 44%, and open drawer from 92.8% to 88%. The claim of substantially higher success across all tasks is contradicted by Table 1.

The active-perception claims exceed what the mechanism provides. TAVP re-renders a point cloud reconstructed from existing camera observations; it does not acquire previously unobserved surfaces by moving physical cameras. It can improve visibility in a projection of already captured geometry, but cannot generally recover information hidden from all input cameras. Furthermore, Eq. (1) and Figure 2 specify only XYZ/RGB input to MVEP, leaving unclear how viewpoint prediction directly conditions on the instruction or task, as the task-aware planning narrative suggests.

TaskMoE's distinctive contributions are insufficiently established. The manuscript does not precisely specify how tasks select among shared gates, how this assignment is learned, or how unseen task IDs are handled. There are no separate ablations of instruction/scene conditioning and shared gating, nor parameter-matched controls or routing analyses. Thus, the evidence does not distinguish the proposed routing mechanisms from increased model capacity or demonstrate reduced task interference.

Important training details remain unresolved despite the appendix. Equation (6) subtracts vectors of action losses without specifying their reduction into a scalar reward; Eq. (9) calls reward weights learnable without describing their objective or update. The PPO objective and key optimization settings are omitted, while reparameterized sampling alone does not justify the stated end-to-end backpropagation claim through rendering. These gaps materially limit reproducibility of the main technical contribution.

Generalization and real-world robustness are only weakly supported. The zero-shot result is three successes in 25 trials on one unseen task, versus zero without TaskMoE, with no uncertainty analysis or clear unseen-ID routing protocol. Real-world results provide selected execution sequences but no aggregate success rates, evaluation counts, or quantitative baseline comparison. They demonstrate feasibility rather than the claimed broad robustness.

Several correctable reporting problems amplify the overstatement: the text gives 86.44% where Table 2 reports 86.67%, attributes an up-to-56-point improvement to comparisons against the strongest baseline although that peg-insertion difference is against RVT2, and claims improvements across all five tasks in sensitivity experiments despite individual regressions. These presentation issues are secondary; the recommendation is driven primarily by missing matched controls and insufficient specification and validation of the proposed mechanisms.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant visual manipulation problem: selecting useful projections of multi-camera observations while reducing interference between tasks. Combining learned virtual viewpoints with task-conditioned expert routing is a potentially useful extension of RVT-2 and ARP.

Table 1 reports 86.7% average success across 18 RLBench tasks, compared with 84.9% for ARP+ and 81.4% for RVT-2. Some improvements are substantial, including insert peg (96.0% versus 78.4%) and sort shape (64.0% versus 46.4%) relative to ARP+.
The demonstration-based pseudo-environment offers a practical way to optimize viewpoints without simulator rollouts. Table 4 reports a modest inference-time increase from 0.394 to 0.436 seconds.

The evaluation includes component ablations, viewpoint sensitivity experiments, and qualitative demonstrations on five physical-robot tasks. The appendix supplies camera configurations, demonstration counts, and several implementation hyperparameters.
weaknesses: The central viewpoint contribution is not convincingly isolated. Table 2 compares learned views against random viewpoints, yielding 86.67% versus 8.89%, but does not report the fixed-view TaskMoE model already trained in Stage 1 under a matched training budget. The random-view condition also ambiguously removes exploration fine-tuning. This comparison cannot establish how much learned view selection improves over sensible fixed projections, independently of training and distribution mismatch. Likewise, removing TaskMoE does not isolate its proposed multimodal routing and shared-gate innovations from additional model capacity.

The main aggregate improvement is insufficiently characterized statistically. The appendix reports 25 evaluation episodes per task, without repeated-seed results or uncertainty estimates. Against that evidence, the 1.8-percentage-point advantage over ARP+ and roughly 1.1-point TaskMoE ablation gain remain tentative. Baseline evaluation and retraining protocols are not sufficiently documented to establish a matched comparison.

The active-perception claims exceed the actual observation model. TAVP re-renders a point cloud reconstructed from existing fixed-camera observations; it does not acquire new measurements or recover surfaces occluded in every input view. It can improve the presentation of already observed geometry, which is valuable, but claims of overcoming missing observations and repositioning cameras obscure this distinction. Moreover, the specified MVEP input in Eq. (1) contains only XYZ and RGB, leaving direct instruction conditioning of the supposedly task-aware viewpoint policy unclear.

Core implementation details remain underspecified. The manuscript does not adequately define task-to-gate assignment, expert architectures and output combination, or the handling of unseen task identifiers. In the reinforcement-learning formulation, Eq. (6) subtracts vectors of losses without specifying their scalar reduction, and Eq. (9) introduces learnable reward weights without an optimization rule. PPO-specific settings and the point-cloud aggregation inside the viewpoint network are also missing. These gaps impede reproduction of the claimed methodological contributions.

Generalization and physical-robot robustness are supported only weakly. The unseen-task result is 12% versus 0% on one task over 25 episodes—three successes versus none—with no uncertainty analysis and unclear unseen-ID routing. The real-world appendix provides execution examples but no quantitative success rates or controlled baseline comparison. These observations support feasibility, but not the manuscript's broad claims of reliable transfer and robustness.

Several interpretations contradict the reported results. TAVP does not outperform ARP+ on every task: stack cups drops from 80% to 60%, and open drawer, place cups, screw bulb, and sweep to dustpan also decline. The stated 56-point gain corresponds to comparison with RVT-2 on insert peg, rather than the strongest ARP+ baseline. Table 3 also contradicts claims that tighter radial bounds and additional views improve every task. These overstatements materially affect the claimed consistency of the benefits; smaller editorial issues, such as the 86.44%/86.67% discrepancy and placeholder bibliography entries, are secondary. Overall, the promising empirical results do not yet outweigh the attribution, reproducibility, and evidential concerns, leading to Weak Reject.

strengths: TAVP addresses a relevant visual manipulation problem by combining learned virtual viewpoints with task-conditioned expert routing. Optimizing rendering viewpoints using demonstration-based action losses is a potentially useful extension of the RVT-2/ARP pipeline.

Table 1 reports 86.7% average success across 18 RLBench tasks versus 84.9% for ARP+, with substantial gains on insert peg (96.0% versus 78.4%) and sort shape (64.0% versus 46.4%). These task-specific improvements are promising.
The reported inference overhead is modest: 0.436 seconds versus 0.394 seconds for ARP+. The pseudo-environment also permits viewpoint training without additional robot interaction.

The manuscript includes component ablations, viewpoint sensitivity experiments, and qualitative demonstrations on five real-world tasks. The appendix provides useful camera, training-data, and implementation details.
weaknesses: The central viewpoint contribution is not cleanly isolated. Table 2 compares learned views with random views while also removing active-exploration fine-tuning; the resulting 8.89% success can reflect unsuitable views or training-distribution mismatch. A fixed-view TaskMoE model with matched training is missing, so this ablation does not establish that learned view planning accounts for the gains over an already effective fixed-view pipeline.

The reliability of the aggregate improvement is unclear. The appendix reports 25 evaluation episodes per task, but no repeated-training results or uncertainty estimates are provided. The 1.8-point average gain over ARP+ accompanies regressions, including stack cups (60% versus 80%). Baseline evaluation and training-budget comparability are insufficiently documented.

Important implementation details remain unspecified: how tasks are assigned to shared gates, how unseen task identifiers are handled, and how the learnable reward weights are optimized. Equation 6 subtracts vectors of losses without defining their scalar aggregation for PPO. These omissions affect reproduction of the proposed mechanisms, beyond ordinary presentation refinements.

The perception claims exceed the demonstrated capability. TAVP re-renders a point cloud reconstructed from the same fixed RGB-D cameras; it can improve the presentation of observed geometry but cannot recover surfaces unseen by all cameras. Claims of acquiring new information or eliminating occlusion need this distinction. Moreover, the specified MVEP input contains XYZ and RGB only, leaving its direct task conditioning unclear.

Evidence for TaskMoE's distinctive routing design and generalization is limited. Removing the entire MoE does not isolate multimodal routing or shared gates from increased model capacity. The unseen-task result is only 3 successes in 25 open-drawer trials versus zero, with no uncertainty analysis. Real-world results are qualitative, without trial counts or comparative success rates.

Several interpretations contradict the tables: TAVP does not outperform ARP+ on every task, and increasing view count does not consistently improve every task in Table 3. The claimed 56-point improvement corresponds to insert peg against RVT2, not ARP+. These correctable reporting issues amplify the broader evidential concerns. Overall, the promising integration and task-specific gains are outweighed by insufficient causal validation and reproducibility of its central contributions.

strengths: The combination of learned virtual viewpoints, task-conditioned expert routing, and autoregressive action prediction addresses a relevant problem in visual robotic manipulation. Optimizing viewpoints using demonstration-based action losses is a potentially useful way to avoid expensive simulator interaction.

Table 1 reports competitive performance across 18 RLBench tasks: approximately 86.6% average success versus 84.9% for ARP+. Gains on Insert Peg (98.0% versus 78.4%) and Sort Shape (62.0% versus 46.4%) are substantial.

The fixed-view ablation provides evidence that learned rendering helps: success increases from 83.33% to 86.67%. Removing TaskMoE reduces performance to 85.56%, providing some support for both components.

The paper includes physical-robot evaluation, sensitivity experiments, and inference timing. The reported real-world improvement over Diffusion Policy is 20 percentage points, while inference latency increases by approximately 10.7% relative to ARP+.
weaknesses: Central implementation details are insufficiently specified for reproduction. Section 3.2 does not explain precisely how tasks select among the shared gates, how routing is trained, or how an unseen task ID is handled. In Section 3.4, Equation 6 defines a vector-valued loss difference without specifying its reduction to a scalar reward, and Equation 9 introduces learnable reward weights without their optimization objective. Appendix B and Table 9 do not resolve these gaps.

The ablations do not establish the claimed mechanisms or distinguish the proposed designs from simpler alternatives. TaskMoE is compared with removal, without a capacity-matched dense model or conventional MoE, and neither multimodal routing nor shared gates is isolated. Viewpoint learning lacks reward-component ablations and an equally fine-tuned random-view control. The 8.89% random-view result therefore does not establish that learned exploration contributes dominantly; the fixed-view comparison supports a more modest 3.34-point gain.

The active-perception and occlusion claims exceed what the method demonstrates. TAVP reprojects a point cloud reconstructed from existing camera observations; it does not acquire previously unobserved surfaces. This can improve representations of already captured geometry, but does not establish recovery from sensor-level occlusion. Moreover, the MVEP input in Equation 1 and Figure 2 contains scene geometry and color, with no explicit instruction input, leaving the claimed task conditioning of viewpoint selection unclear.

Uncertainty and comparison protocols are not sufficiently documented to assess the modest aggregate improvement. The number of training seeds and the meaning of the reported standard deviations are unspecified, and the main ablations lack uncertainty estimates. Claims of superiority across all tasks contradict Table 1: TAVP falls below ARP+ on several tasks, including Put in Safe (78.0% versus 86.4%) and Stack Cups (64.0% versus 80.0%).

Generalization and robustness conclusions are substantially stronger than the evidence. Unseen-task transfer is evaluated only on Open Drawer, with 3 successes in 25 episodes versus zero. Real-world robustness uses 10 trials per condition on one task; under heavy occlusion, TAVP succeeds only twice versus once for Diffusion Policy. These results are preliminary evidence, rather than convincing support for broad transfer or effective occlusion handling.

Several reporting discrepancies weaken interpretability. Table 8 reports 52% success for TAVP on Put in Cupboard with 100 demonstrations, versus 74% in Table 1, without explaining the experimental difference. Figure 5 identifies ARP+ as the physical-robot baseline, whereas quantitative real-world comparisons use Diffusion Policy. The appendix's five illustrated real-world tasks also do not match the evaluated task list. Overall, the promising benchmark results are outweighed by unresolved methodological specification and attribution concerns, rather than by limited evaluation breadth alone.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant visual manipulation problem: selecting useful projections of multi-camera RGB-D observations while learning task-sensitive representations. Combining learned virtual viewpoints with a coarse-to-fine manipulation policy is potentially useful.

Table 1 reports competitive results across 18 RLBench tasks: approximately 86.7% average success versus 84.9% for ARP+. Some improvements are substantial, including Insert Peg (98.0% versus 78.4%) and Sort Shape (62.0% versus 46.4%).

The fixed-view ablation provides evidence that learned viewpoints help: success increases from 83.33% to 86.67%. Removing TaskMoE reduces performance to 85.56%, supporting a smaller additional contribution.

Real-world experiments extend the evidence beyond simulation: TAVP achieves 88% average success versus 68% for Diffusion Policy across five tasks. Reported inference overhead relative to ARP+ is modest, increasing from 0.394 to 0.436 seconds.
The manuscript includes supplementary algorithm descriptions, camera parameterization, demonstration counts, and implementation settings, as well as sensitivity and robustness experiments.
weaknesses: The central active-perception claim exceeds what the method implements. Section 3 and Appendix B reconstruct a point cloud from existing camera observations and select virtual rendering poses; they do not acquire additional sensor observations. Reprojection can expose already-observed geometry more effectively to the policy, but cannot recover surfaces hidden from all input cameras. Statements about repositioning cameras, acquiring more complete observations, and overcoming occlusion need this distinction. No direct visibility or occlusion analysis establishes the claimed mechanism, and real-world heavy-occlusion success remains only 20% in Table 7.

Important elements of the proposed method remain underspecified. TaskMoE lacks a precise definition of task-to-gate assignment, expert architecture and aggregation, and handling of an unseen task identifier. MVEP is explicitly defined as receiving XYZ and RGB, while its claimed instruction-dependent viewpoint selection is not explained by that input specification or Figure 2. These omissions affect both reproducibility and assessment of the task-aware contribution.

The reward and optimization procedure are not fully defined even with the appendix. Equation 6 produces a vector of four loss differences, whereas Equation 9 treats it as a reward component without specifying scalarization. The weights are described as learnable, but their objective and update procedure are absent, despite the statement that only MVEP is trainable in Stage 2. Algorithm 1 constructs independent observation-action-reward tuples without explaining the PPO return/advantage calculation, and Table 9 omits central PPO settings. This prevents confident reconstruction of the main learning algorithm.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed architectural innovations sufficiently. The 1.11-point TaskMoE gain is not accompanied by parameter-matched controls or separate tests of multimodal routing and shared gates. The random-view result of 8.89% is difficult to interpret because training and post-training treatment of that variant are unclear; it may reflect a severe distribution shift. The fixed-view comparison is more informative, but reward-component and simpler viewpoint-selection controls are absent.

The reliability and scope of the empirical gains are overstated. The main aggregate improvement over ARP+ is approximately 1.8 points, but the number of independent runs and aggregate uncertainty are unspecified. Contrary to the claim of improvement across all tasks, Table 1 includes regressions such as Stack Cups (64% versus 80%) and Put in Safe (78% versus 86.4%). Similarly, increasing the view count does not improve every task in Table 3. These are substantive misinterpretations of reported evidence, rather than merely stylistic issues.

Generalization and real-world comparisons provide preliminary rather than strong support for the broader claims. Zero-shot generalization is tested on one task, with 12% success over 25 trials—three successes—and no stated unseen-ID protocol. Real-world evaluation uses ten trials per task and compares quantitatively only against Diffusion Policy, leaving the contributions of view planning and TaskMoE unisolated. These limitations would not independently justify rejection, but together with the central specification and attribution gaps, they make the current balance favor weak rejection despite the promising benchmark results.

strengths: The paper addresses a relevant visual manipulation problem: choosing useful projections of fused RGB-D observations. Combining learned virtual viewpoints with task-conditioned expert routing is a potentially useful extension of RVT-2/ARP-style policies.

The evaluation provides meaningful positive evidence across 18 RLBench tasks. TAVP achieves approximately 86.7% average success versus 84.9% for ARP+, with substantial gains on Insert Peg (98.0% versus 78.4%) and Sort Shape (62.0% versus 46.4%).

The fixed-view ablation supports the usefulness of viewpoint optimization: success increases from 83.33% to 86.67%. Removing TaskMoE reduces success to 85.56%, suggesting a smaller complementary benefit.

Physical deployment strengthens the practical contribution: across five tasks with 50 demonstrations per task, TAVP achieves 88% success versus 68% for Diffusion Policy. Reported inference latency increases moderately, from 0.394 to 0.436 seconds relative to ARP+.

The manuscript includes camera parameterization, a training-stage description, supplementary pseudo-environment pseudocode, and sensitivity experiments, providing a useful foundation for understanding the implementation.
weaknesses: The central perception claim exceeds what the method establishes. TAVP re-renders a point cloud reconstructed from existing camera observations; it does not acquire previously unseen surfaces through physical camera movement. It can improve projection and expose information already captured by another sensor, but cannot recover geometry hidden from all input cameras. Claims of overcoming or eliminating occlusion need this distinction, especially given only 20% success under heavy occlusion in Table 7.

Important mechanisms remain underspecified. Section 3.2 does not precisely define gate selection, expert architecture, routing optimization, or handling of unseen task IDs. Equation 6 defines a vector of loss differences, but its reduction into the scalar reward is unclear; the optimization of the learnable reward weights is also unspecified. The appendix supplies generic training settings but omits key PPO settings. These gaps materially limit reproducibility of the proposed components.

The ablations do not isolate the claimed architectural innovations sufficiently. There are no comparisons against conventional MoE routing or capacity-matched dense models, nor separate tests of instruction/vision conditioning and shared gates. The random-view result of 8.89% is difficult to interpret without knowing whether the action model was trained to accommodate those views. The fixed-view comparison is more informative, but matched training budgets and post-training procedures are not established.

The main improvement over ARP+ is modest and its reliability is unclear: the number of independent runs and aggregate uncertainty are not reported. Gains are also uneven, with regressions on Put in Safe (78.0% versus 86.4%) and Stack Cups (64.0% versus 80.0%). Statements that TAVP improves across all tasks contradict Table 1. Real-world comparisons use only 10 trials per task and do not quantitatively compare against the closest RVT-2/ARP family.

Generalization evidence is preliminary. Table 6 evaluates only one unseen task, Open Drawer, with 12% success over 25 episodes—three successes—versus zero without TaskMoE. This does not convincingly establish broad task transfer or the proposed discovery of semantic task clusters. Moreover, MVEP's specified input is only the colored point cloud, leaving direct instruction conditioning of viewpoint selection unclear.

Overall, the benchmark gains, fixed-view ablation, and physical experiments support a worthwhile contribution. However, incomplete specification and insufficient isolation of the proposed mechanisms leave the scientific case near the acceptance boundary; the concern is attribution and technical support, rather than merely limited benchmark breadth.
